questions.q: In which year did the Hijra (migration of the Prophet and his followers from Mecca to Medina) occur, and why does this date mark the beginning of the Islamic calendar?
questions.a: The Hijra occurred in 622 CE. This date marks the Islamic calendar's beginning (1 AH) because it represents the transition from a persecuted religious movement to a self-governing political community (Ummah) with territorial sovereignty in Medina. A wrong answer (e.g., 610 CE — first revelation, or 630 CE — conquest of Mecca) reveals the student confuses the *spiritual inception* of Islam with its *political institutionalization*, missing the historical significance of the Hijra as the moment the Muslim community became a distinct polity.

questions.q: The Prophet Muhammad's early preaching in Mecca (610–622 CE) focused on Tawhid (monotheism) and social justice. Explain why the Quraysh elite opposed him, linking their economic interests to their religious authority.
questions.a: The Quraysh elite opposed the Prophet because Tawhid threatened the pilgrimage economy centered on the Ka'ba's 360 idols — Mecca's religious plurality attracted tribes for trade fairs, generating revenue for Quraysh merchants. Additionally, the Prophet's condemnation of usury (riba) and demand for wealth redistribution (Zakat) challenged the merchant oligarchy's profits. A wrong answer focusing only on "religious intolerance" or "polytheism vs monotheism" misses the *political economy* of Mecca: the Quraysh were not merely defending theology but protecting a lucrative pilgrimage-trade nexus that sustained their tribal hegemony.

questions.q: Analyze the Constitution of Medina (Sahifat al-Madina) as a political document. Identify three ways it redefined loyalty and governance beyond tribal kinship (asabiyya).
questions.a: The Constitution of Medina redefined loyalty by: (1) establishing the *Ummah* as a supra-tribal community where membership was based on faith (Muslims) or treaty (Jews, pagans), not blood; (2) making the Prophet the supreme arbiter of disputes, replacing tribal vengeance with centralized adjudication; (3) imposing collective security — "the believers are protectors of one another" — so an attack on one clan was an attack on all. A weak answer lists only "religious unity" or "peace treaty" without showing how the document *mechanically* replaced tribal customary law with a written constitutional order, a precedent for later Islamic governance.

questions.q: Compare the Battle of Badr (624 CE) and the Battle of Uhud (625 CE) in terms of their strategic outcomes for the Muslim community's legitimacy in Arabia. Why did a military defeat at Uhud not destroy the Prophet's authority?
questions.a: Badr (Muslim victory, 313 vs 950) established Muslim military credibility, boosted morale, and attracted tribal allies; Uhud (Muslim defeat due to archer disobedience) tested but did not break the community because: (1) the Prophet's leadership survived — he was wounded but rallied troops; (2) the Quraysh failed to capitalize — they withdrew without destroying Medina; (3) the Quranic response (Surah Al-Imran) framed the defeat as a test of faith, not divine abandonment, reinforcing ideological cohesion. A student who sees Uhud as mere "failure" misses how *narrative management* of setbacks strengthened the Prophet's charismatic authority — a pattern repeated in later Islamic history (e.g., early Delhi Sultanate setbacks).

questions.q: Evaluate the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (628 CE) as a diplomatic masterstroke. Why did many companions initially view it as a humiliation, and how did it prove strategically decisive within two years?
questions.a: Companions saw Hudaybiyyah as humiliation because it accepted Quraysh terms: no pilgrimage that year, 10-year truce, and any Meccan Muslim fleeing to Medina must be returned (but not vice versa). Yet it was decisive because: (1) it forced Quraysh to recognize Muslims as *political equals* negotiating a treaty; (2) the truce allowed Muslim expansion northward (Khaybar conquest); (3) the "return clause" collapsed when Muslim women sought refuge — Quran 60:10 abrogated it, exposing Quraysh bad faith; (4) within two years, Quraysh violated the truce (Banu Bakr attack on Khuza'a), giving the Prophet justification for the bloodless conquest of Mecca (630). A poor answer calls it "compromise" without analyzing how *apparent concession created strategic space* — a core concept in statecraft.

questions.q: Construct a timeline of the Prophet's life (570–632 CE) with 8 key events. For each event, annotate whether it was primarily *spiritual*, *political*, *military*, or *social* in significance — and explain why the conquest of Mecca (630 CE) synthesizes all four dimensions.
questions.a: Timeline: 570 Birth (social — orphanhood shaped empathy); 610 First Revelation (spiritual); 613 Public Preaching (social/spiritual); 615 First Hijra to Abyssinia (political — seeking asylum); 622 Hijra to Medina (political — state founding); 624 Badr (military); 627 Trench (military/political); 628 Hudaybiyyah (political/diplomatic); 630 Conquest of Mecca (synthesis: spiritual — Ka'ba purified; political — Quraysh submission; military — bloodless entry; social — general amnesty unified tribe and faith); 632 Farewell Pilgrimage & Death (spiritual/social — final sermon on equality). A weak answer lists events without *categorical annotation* or fails to show how 630 CE was the *culmination* where the Prophet's roles as messenger, statesman, general, and reformer converged — the template for later "commander of the faithful" (Amir al-Mu'minin).
